# Sail examples

> Runnable examples of Spark SQL and DataFrame code on Sail, an engine that runs Spark code over
> Spark Connect. Every example that uses only Spark APIs is checked to return the same result on
> Apache Spark and on Sail, except the Iceberg example, which is checked against an independent
> reference.

Things to remember when using Sail (checked against pysail==0.7.3 with pyspark-client==4.1.3):

- Connect to Sail with a normal PySpark Spark Connect session. In a script, start Sail in-process with `pysail.spark.SparkConnectServer()`, call `start()`, read the port from `server.listening_address`, and connect with `SparkSession.builder.remote(f"sc://localhost:{port}")`. As a long-running service, run `sail spark server` (default `127.0.0.1:50051`, per the Sail docs). `SELECT version()` returns the Sail version; `spark.version` returns the PySpark client's version.
- `sail spark run -f script.py` (or `-f -` to read the script from stdin) starts a temporary Sail server, runs the script with a ready `spark` session, and stops the server. A `WARN ... aborting N task(s)` line at exit is harmless.
- With the lightweight `pyspark-client` package, `pyspark.testing.assertDataFrameEqual` fails before comparing anything (it imports pandas-on-Spark and looks for a local Spark installation). In tests against Sail, compare collected rows instead, for example `sorted(map(tuple, df.collect())) == expected`.
- `collect()` returns `TIMESTAMP` values as Python datetimes in the client process's local time zone, whatever `spark.sql.session.timeZone` is; `TIMESTAMP_NTZ` values come back unchanged. Store wall-clock values as `TIMESTAMP_NTZ` (for example `to_timestamp_ntz`), or compare instants, so tests do not depend on the machine they run on.
- Set Sail engine options as `SAIL_<SECTION>__<KEY>` environment variables before the server starts, for example `SAIL_EXECUTION__DEFAULT_PARALLELISM=8`. `spark.conf.set` changes only the Spark SQL session options Sail maps, such as `spark.sql.session.timeZone`; `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` has no effect.
- Configure catalogs with the `SAIL_CATALOG__LIST` environment variable (a TOML array) and `SAIL_CATALOG__DEFAULT_CATALOG` before the server starts; the Sail catalog docs cover Iceberg REST, Unity, Glue and Hive Metastore entries. JVM-style `spark.sql.catalog.<name>` settings do not create catalogs.
- With no catalog configured, the current catalog is named `sail`, not `spark_catalog`. Avoid hard-coding `spark_catalog` in three-part table names.
- To reuse an expensive result without writing a table yourself, set `SAIL_EXECUTION__CHECKPOINT__PATH` to a directory before the server starts and call `df.checkpoint()`; the returned DataFrame is not recomputed by later actions.
- In local mode (the default), Python UDFs run inside the Sail server process, in one Python interpreter shared by all tasks, while Apache Spark runs them in separate Python worker processes. Prefer built-in functions, and for CPU-heavy Python work prefer libraries that release the GIL (NumPy, PyArrow compute, ONNX Runtime, tokenizers) so tasks can overlap.
- In local mode, Sail runs the partitions of a Python UDF at the same time as threads of the server process (Apache Spark uses separate Python worker processes). A library that must not be called from two threads at once (PDFium through pypdfium2, per its docs) therefore needs one lock for the whole process. Keep that lock in `sys.modules`, which every task and every later query in the process share. A global of your script will not do: its functions are pickled by value, so each task gets its own copy of the globals.
- To load a model or client once per partition, put the setup before the loop in `mapInArrow`, `mapInPandas` or an iterator `pandas_udf`. In an iterator `arrow_udf`, code before the loop runs once per batch instead.
- Build `mapInArrow` output batches with an Arrow schema that matches the declared schema exactly (int32 for `int`, int64 for `long`), for example `pa.RecordBatch.from_pydict(rows, schema=...)`. Sail accepts an int64 column declared as `int`, but Apache Spark fails on it, so code that relies on the leniency is not portable.
- As in Spark, a deterministic Python UDF can run more than once per row when the query filters on its output. Mark UDFs that are expensive or have side effects (model or API calls) with `.asNondeterministic()`, which makes them run once per row.
- Create UDFs after the Spark session exists. With PySpark 4 clients, `@udf`, `@pandas_udf` and `@arrow_udf` applied at import time, before any session, fail with `NO_ACTIVE_OR_DEFAULT_SESSION` (or `SESSION_OR_CONTEXT_NOT_EXISTS`). Keep plain functions at module level and wrap them, for example `F.udf(fn, "double")`, once the session is up.
- The number of rows `mapInArrow` and `mapInPandas` receive per batch is capped by the `SAIL_EXECUTION__BATCH_SIZE` environment variable, set before the server starts (default 8192 per the Sail configuration docs); `spark.sql.execution.arrow.maxRecordsPerBatch` has no effect. Lower it for wide rows such as images, documents or embeddings.
- `spark.addArtifacts()` is not supported, so Python files and packages cannot be shipped from the client at run time. Install every library your UDFs import into the Python environment the Sail server runs in.
- Sail reads and writes Delta Lake with no extra package: `format("delta")` writes (`partitionBy`, append, `replaceWhere`), `CREATE TABLE ... USING delta`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `MERGE INTO`, time travel (`versionAsOf`, `VERSION AS OF`), `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMNS`, `DESCRIBE HISTORY`, `OPTIMIZE` and `VACUUM`. A `mergeSchema` append of computed (nullable) values also adds a column to a table created with `CREATE TABLE t (...) USING delta`. `RESTORE` is not supported; read the old version with `versionAsOf` instead. Apache Spark needs `delta-spark` with its session extension and catalog (per the Delta Lake docs).
- To process loose files (images, PDFs, audio, documents), build a DataFrame of file paths and read each file inside `mapInArrow` or a pandas UDF, returning only what later stages need (text, features, embeddings). This gives exactly one row per file and keeps large binaries out of the data passed between stages. Paths must be readable from where the UDF runs (local files on one machine, object storage on a cluster).
- Parquet, CSV, JSON, text and Delta Lake read and write with the standard `spark.read` and `df.write` calls and need no extra packages. Avro can be read but not written. ORC (read or write) and the `image` source are not available.
- Sail reads and writes Apache Iceberg tables with no extra package: `format("iceberg")` writes to a path (including `partitionBy`, append and overwrite), `CREATE TABLE ... USING iceberg LOCATION`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `MERGE INTO`, and time travel to a snapshot with `option("snapshot-id", id)` or `VERSION AS OF id`. The metadata tables `t.snapshots` and `t.history` list the snapshot ids. In a table created with `PARTITIONED BY`, Sail lists the partition columns last; select columns by name.
- A Python data source's partitions are read as separate tasks, so `read()` calls for different partitions run at the same time. Return one partition per page, file or key range to fetch an API or a set of files concurrently.
- Inferred schemas differ from Apache Spark's in three ways: CSV `inferSchema` reads whole numbers as `BIGINT` (Spark: `INT`); JSON keeps columns in file order (Spark sorts them by name); and partition columns of a partitioned directory come back as strings (Spark infers numbers and dates). Pass an explicit schema (`spark.read.schema(...)`) when types or column order matter.
- The JSON reader's `multiLine` option is not supported: JSON Lines files read correctly, but a pretty-printed JSON document fails to parse. Convert such files to JSON Lines, or read each file through a table of paths and parse it with `json.loads` inside a UDF.
- Query files in place with `` FROM parquet.`path` ``, `` csv.`path` `` or `` json.`path` ``, where the path is a file, a folder, or a glob such as `data/2024-*.parquet` that reads every matching file as one table. A CSV file queried this way is read without a header: its first line is a data row and the columns are `_c0`, `_c1`, and so on. For a header and declared types, create a view: `CREATE TEMPORARY VIEW v (a INT, b STRING) USING csv OPTIONS (path '...', header 'true')`.
- `pyspark.ml` (MLlib) is not available, although Spark Connect 4.x supports it. Train and score models with Python libraries (scikit-learn, PyTorch, ONNX Runtime) inside `mapInArrow` or a pandas UDF, or outside the engine.
- `spark.sparkContext` and the RDD API are not available, as on any Spark Connect server. Use the DataFrame and SQL APIs instead, for example `spark.createDataFrame([], schema)` rather than `sparkContext.emptyRDD()`.
- A few Spark SQL clauses need another form on Sail: filter on `row_number()` in a subquery instead of `QUALIFY`; use `df.groupBy(...).pivot(col, values)` instead of the SQL `PIVOT` clause; number sessions with `lag` and a running `sum` instead of `session_window`. `CACHE TABLE` and `UNCACHE TABLE` are not supported; save the result to Parquet and read it back instead.
- Structured Streaming support is partial: `writeStream.foreachBatch()` fails and the `memory` sink is not available, while both work on Apache Spark. Check the Sail streaming docs before porting a streaming job.
- Sail does not support dynamic partition overwrite for Parquet: with `partitionOverwriteMode` set to `dynamic` (in the session or as a writer option), `df.write.mode("overwrite").partitionBy(c)` still replaces every partition of the path, and `INSERT OVERWRITE` replaces the whole table, where Apache Spark replaces only the partitions the data contains. Delta Lake tables follow the setting on both engines. `INSERT OVERWRITE t PARTITION (c = value)` is not supported. To replace one Parquet partition, overwrite its own directory (`path/c=value`, without the partition column), or write Delta Lake.
- Use `dayofweek(d)` (Sunday 1 to Saturday 7) for the day of the week: it agrees on Sail and Apache Spark. The other forms differ on Sail, for dates and timestamps alike: `EXTRACT(DOW FROM d)` and `date_part('dow', d)` count from Sunday = 0 (Spark: 1), `weekday(d)` returns -1 for Sunday (Spark: 6; Monday to Saturday agree, 0 to 5), and `EXTRACT(DAYOFWEEK FROM d)` and `EXTRACT(DOW_ISO FROM d)` are not supported.
- In regular expressions (`regexp_replace`, `regexp_extract`, `rlike`, `split`), Sail's `\s`, `\d` and `\w` match Unicode characters (an ideographic space, an Arabic-Indic digit, `é`), while Apache Spark's match ASCII only, so the same pattern can return different results on non-ASCII text. For the same results on both, write the class you mean: `[ \t\n\r]`, `[0-9]` and `[A-Za-z0-9_]` for ASCII, or `[\p{Z}\t\n\r]`, `\p{Nd}` and `[\p{L}\p{Nd}_]` for Unicode. The `(?U)` flag is not a portable switch: Spark reads it as Unicode classes, Sail as lazy quantifiers.
- Approximate and random results can differ from Apache Spark's: `percentile_approx`, `approx_count_distinct`, the percentiles from `df.summary()`, and the rows chosen by `sample(fraction, seed)` and `randomSplit(weights, seed)`. With the same seed, `sample` and `randomSplit` pick the same rows again on Sail, but not the rows Spark picks. When results must match, use `percentile`, `median`, `count(DISTINCT ...)`, and a deterministic filter on a hash of a key (`hash` and `xxhash64` return the same values on both).
- `date_trunc(unit, ts)` on a `TIMESTAMP_NTZ` column (the type Parquet timestamps without a time zone are read as) returns `TIMESTAMP_NTZ` on Sail but `TIMESTAMP` on Apache Spark. So the column type in files written from it differs, and collected values can differ when the client's local time zone is not the session time zone. Cast the result (`CAST(date_trunc('MONTH', ts) AS TIMESTAMP_NTZ)`) or truncate a date (`trunc(date(ts), 'MM')`), which give the same type and value on both.
- Dividing DECIMAL values gives a different result type on Sail than on Apache Spark (sometimes fewer, sometimes more decimal places), and Sail truncates where Spark rounds. `7 / 60.0` is 0.1166 on Sail and 0.116667 on Spark; `CAST(2 AS DECIMAL(10,0)) / CAST(3 AS DECIMAL(10,0))` is 0.6666 and 0.66666666667. A literal with a decimal point, such as `60.0`, is a DECIMAL. For the same results on both, divide DOUBLE values (`x / 60.0D`, `CAST(x AS DOUBLE) / y`) or integers (`x / 60`, which returns a DOUBLE on both), and round explicitly when you need a fixed number of digits.
- `cache()` and `persist()` are accepted but do not keep results: every action recomputes the DataFrame, including any UDF or model call in it. To reuse an expensive result (for example model outputs), write it to Parquet or a table and read it back.
- For embeddings, store vectors as `ARRAY<FLOAT>` and use `vector_cosine_similarity`, `vector_inner_product` and `vector_l2_distance` (Spark 4.2 has them too). Both engines reject `ARRAY<DOUBLE>`; Sail also rejects Arrow fixed-size lists (as written by NumPy or PyArrow), which Spark accepts. `CAST(col AS ARRAY<FLOAT>)` first.
- Sail adds SQL functions that call TypeSafe's Jev models: `jev_noul`, `jev_choice`, `jev_score`, `jev_system_one` and `jev_models` (Apache Spark has none of them). They need a non-empty `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` in the Sail server's environment, and on a cluster in every worker that runs Jev calls (per the Sail Jev docs); with an empty key a call fails with an error that names the variable. The calls send row values to the TypeSafe API (per the Sail Jev docs).
- A Jev function asks one question per row it evaluates. Adjacent rows with the same text share one request, but each row is still its own question, and the same text in rows that are not adjacent is sent again. Apply Jev to `SELECT DISTINCT` inputs, save the answers, and join them back to ask once per distinct value. The endpoint comes from `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL` (per the Sail Jev docs).

## Examples

- [Hello Sail](quickstart/hello-sail/README.md): Use when you want to run existing Spark SQL and DataFrame code on your laptop with Sail, with no Java and no cluster.
- [Query Parquet and CSV files with SQL](quickstart/query-files-with-sql/README.md): Use when you want to explore data files on your laptop with plain SQL (query a Parquet or CSV file in place, name files as views, join, group and sort) without loading a database or starting a cluster.
- [Explore a year of taxi trips with SQL](analytics/explore-taxi-trips/README.md): Use when you want to analyze a real dataset on your laptop with SQL (read a folder of Parquet files as one table, filter out bad records, trend by month, find peak hours, compute exact medians and percentiles, rank within groups).
- [Reconcile orders, captures and refunds](analytics/reconcile-orders-payments/README.md): Use when separate order and payment feeds contain repeated deliveries, split captures, partial refunds or orphan transactions, and you need an explainable reconciliation at an explicit cutoff.
- [Reproduce a report from saved Iceberg snapshots](analytics/reproduce-iceberg-report/README.md): Use when a sales report joins changing Iceberg tables and you need to record its exact input snapshot pair, then replay the original logical rows in another process.
- [Sessions, funnels and cohort retention with SQL](analytics/sessions-funnels-retention/README.md): Use when you analyze event or clickstream data and need sessions from exact time gaps, an ordered session-scoped conversion funnel, or weekly cohort retention that distinguishes observed inactivity from future weeks.
- [Use SQL inside a Python app with pandas](analytics/sql-in-a-python-app/README.md): Use when a Python program (a script, a service, a notebook) keeps data in pandas and you want to query it with SQL, safely parameterized, and get pandas or Arrow results back.
- [Turn spoken requests into intent analytics](analytics/support-intent-analytics/README.md): Use when you want to transcribe short spoken requests, compare intent predictions with labels, and aggregate the results with SQL.
- [Apply replayed changes without resurrecting deleted records](pipelines/apply-versioned-changes/README.md): Use when captured change batches contain retries, stale updates and deletes, and you need a current-state table that retains version barriers and quarantines conflicting equal-version payloads.
- [Build features as they were known at each decision](pipelines/build-point-in-time-features/README.md): Use when reconstructing demand-planning inputs from order revisions and product history, so late arrivals and later corrections cannot leak into earlier decisions.
- [Upsert into a Delta Lake table with MERGE](pipelines/delta-merge-upsert/README.md): Use when you need to apply a batch of changes (updates, inserts and deletes) to a Delta Lake table with one MERGE INTO statement, and read the table as it was before.
- [Manage a Delta Lake table through its life](pipelines/delta-table-lifecycle/README.md): Use when you maintain a Delta Lake table over time (declare it, append, add a column, rebuild one partition, update, delete, merge late corrections) and want to check time travel across the versions this example creates.
- [Build a versioned search evaluation dataset](pipelines/evaluate-search-dataset/README.md): Use when you need to curate versioned documents, queries and relevance judgments, compare two retrieval methods, and validate a Parquet snapshot with a dataset loader.
- [Manage an Apache Iceberg table and read old snapshots](pipelines/iceberg-tables/README.md): Use when you keep data in an Apache Iceberg table on Sail and need to create it with a declared partitioned schema, insert, update, delete and merge rows, and read any earlier snapshot by its id.
- [Normalize nested order events without losing rejected records](pipelines/normalize-order-events/README.md): Use when a bounded JSONL snapshot needs strict order and child validation, separate clean order and line tables, and original rejected records with source identity.
- [Reconcile invoice documents against purchase orders](pipelines/reconcile-invoice-documents/README.md): Use when a small set of known invoice layouts needs real CPU OCR followed by supplier, duplicate, currency and gross purchase-order checks, with explicit exceptions and a structured-input baseline.
- [Repair daily reports after corrected order records](pipelines/repair-daily-reports/README.md): Use when corrected orders, cancellations and deletes change already reported store totals, and a retry must also repair the old store and date after an interrupted source update.
- [Build a batch ETL job with data quality checks](pipelines/taxi-etl-job/README.md): Use when you build a batch pipeline that turns raw files into clean, partitioned Parquet and reporting tables, preserves original rejected records with their source provenance, removes clean duplicates, and replaces one month's outputs on a completed re-run.
- [Read a REST API as a table](python/rest-api-as-a-table/README.md): Use when you want to query a paginated REST API with Spark SQL and DataFrames by writing a Python data source that fetches pages in parallel.
- [Choose a Python UDF style](python/udf-styles/README.md): Use when you need Python logic in a Spark query and want to pick between built-in functions, a row UDF, a pandas UDF, an Arrow UDF and mapInArrow.
- [Embed text and search it with vector functions](ai/embed-and-search/README.md): Use when you want to compute text embeddings inside the engine with an ONNX model and find the most similar documents with SQL vector functions.
- [Enrich a table with a model](ai/enrich-with-a-model/README.md): Use when you need a model's answer for every row of a large table and want to pay for one model call per distinct value, not per row.
- [Route support tickets with a model in SQL (Jev)](ai/jev-sql-routing/README.md): Use when you want to classify table rows with a model from plain SQL on Sail, using the built-in Jev functions, and call the model once per distinct value.
- [Maintain document embeddings as sources change](ai/maintain-document-embeddings/README.md): Use when you need to update a local embedding table after documents are added, edited or removed, while reusing compatible vectors for unchanged content.
- [Align robot camera frames with state and actions](multimodal/align-robot-camera-frames/README.md): Use when robot demonstrations store camera video separately from state/action records and you need sampled frames joined to nearby state timestamps with alignment errors and unmatched frames visible.
- [Classify images with an ONNX model](multimodal/classify-images/README.md): Use when you need to label a folder of images with a pretrained image classifier (batch inference in ONNX Runtime) inside the engine, and send low-confidence predictions to review.
- [Curate robot demonstration episodes](multimodal/curate-robot-episodes/README.md): Use when you need to check robot demonstration records for missing frames, duplicate frames, timestamp gaps and invalid state/action vectors before selecting whole episodes for training and validation.
- [Make thumbnails from a folder of images](multimodal/image-thumbnails/README.md): Use when you need to process a folder of image files (decode, resize, extract metadata) with Python in the engine, one row per file, without moving image bytes between stages.
- [Extract text from scanned PDFs with OCR](multimodal/ocr-scanned-pdfs/README.md): Use when you need the text of scanned or image-only PDFs (no text layer) inside the engine, one row per page with an explicit status for blank pages and unreadable files, using OCR on the CPU (RapidOCR with ONNX Runtime), and want to measure OCR accuracy in SQL.
- [Search a folder of PDFs](multimodal/pdf-search/README.md): Use when you need to turn PDF documents into searchable text chunks with embeddings (extract, chunk, embed, search) inside the engine, one row per file in and small rows out.
- [Search photos by text with CLIP](multimodal/search-images-by-text/README.md): Use when you want to find photos that match a plain-language description, by embedding images and text with CLIP (ONNX) inside the engine and ranking them with SQL vector functions, and to measure retrieval quality in SQL.
- [Find scenes in videos with text search](multimodal/search-video-frames/README.md): Use when you need to search inside video files by description, by sampling frames, embedding them with CLIP (ONNX) inside the engine, splitting videos into scenes with SQL window functions, and ranking scenes per text query.
- [Transcribe audio files with Whisper](multimodal/transcribe-audio/README.md): Use when you need speech-to-text for a folder of audio files inside the engine (Whisper on CPU with faster-whisper), one transcript per file, and want to score the transcripts against references in SQL.
- [Test Spark code with pytest on Sail](migrate/test-spark-code-with-pytest/README.md): Use when you want local unit tests for Spark DataFrame code in pytest, with a Sail session fixture and no Java.
